name: Man Buddha Temple
significance: A Theravada Buddhist temple at Sale in Myanmar's Magway Region that enshrines the Shinbin Maha Laba Man Buddha, a hollow gold-lacquered figure of about 20 feet said to be the largest lacquer Buddha image in the country. The image itself is dated to around 1300.
story: The image is said to have floated downriver from Monywa to Sale during the great floods of 1888.

name: Bút Tháp Temple
significance: A Buddhist temple beside the Đuống River dyke in Bắc Ninh province, founded in the 13th century but whose surviving architecture, sculpture and decoration all belong to the 17th century, when the Zen master Chuyet Chuyet made it famous. Its ten buildings run for about 100 metres and hold a celebrated thousand-armed, thousand-eyed Quan Âm alongside the Buddha triad, Manjushri and Samantabhadra.

name: Quán Sứ Pagoda
deity: The Buddha (front hall); Master Minh Không (rear hall)
significance: A 15th-century Buddhist pagoda on Quan Su Street in central Hanoi, raised on the grounds of a Lê-dynasty guest house built for envoys from Champa and Laos, who as Buddhists wanted a place of worship on the premises. Renovated in 1822, it now serves as the headquarters of the Buddhist Sangha of Vietnam.

name: Changangkha Lhakhang
significance: One of Thimphu's oldest temples, set on a ridge above the city and founded in the 13th or 14th century by Nyima, a son of Phajo Drugom Zhigpo who brought the Drukpa Kagyu teachings to Bhutan. Its bronze Avalokiteshvara is the main image, and the protector Genyen Domtsangpa is invoked as the birth deity of children born at the national referral hospital below.
story: Some hold that the bronze Avalokiteshvara arose of itself rather than being carved, while others credit a Newar master craftsman working at the time the temple was built.

name: Kwan Im Thong Hood Cho Temple
deity: Guanyin (Kuan Yim), worshipped here in her Cundi form
significance: A Chinese Buddhist temple on Waterloo Street in Singapore's Rochor district, begun in 1884 after the firm Chen Liang Cheng gave the land, and rebuilt in 1895 and again in 1980. Its image of Cundi, a form of Guanyin, draws crowds of worshippers seeking good fortune.

name: Payathonzu Temple
significance: A late 13th-century brick temple at Minnanthu, southeast of Bagan, whose Burmese name means Temple of Three Buddhas: three shrines joined by narrow passages, left unfinished by its builders. Its interior murals are noted for Mahayana and Tantric elements unusual in Bagan.

name: Shwesandaw Pagoda
significance: The tallest pagoda at Bagan, raised in 1057 by King Anawrahta to enshrine hair relics of the Buddha brought from Thaton. Five receding terraces, once faced with terracotta Jataka plaques, carry a cylindrical stupa whose jewelled hti was thrown down by the earthquake of 1975.

name: Laung Bwann Brauk Pagoda
significance: A Mrauk U stupa built in 1525 under King Min Khaung Raza and renovated in 1625 by King Thiri Thudhamma, rising through eight octagonal tiers to five tapering ones. Sixteen Buddha images sit in niches on the first tier, and the name, meaning coloured tile, comes from the sixty glazed petals in red, yellow, blue and green set into the square stone wall around it.

name: Buduruvagala
deity: Standing Buddha, flanked by Avalokiteshvara, Tara, Maitreya and Vajrapani
significance: A group of seven colossal figures carved into a rock face near Wellawaya in southern Sri Lanka, dated by most authorities to the 9th or 10th century. The central standing Buddha is the island's tallest, and the flanking bodhisattvas mark the site as a rare surviving Mahayana monument in a Theravada country.
story: A hollow carved into the same rock is said to weep a mustard-scented oil that no one has been able to trace to a source.

name: Seruwila Mangala Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Forehead relic (Lalata Dhatu) and hair relics of Gautama Buddha
significance: An Early Anuradhapura-period stupa in Trincomalee District built by King Kavantissa, and the only site known to enshrine the Buddha's forehead bone relic along with hair relics. It counts as the ninth of the Solosmasthana, the sixteen holiest Buddhist pilgrimage places in Sri Lanka, and its four carved guardstones are unmatched at any other Sri Lankan stupa.
story: The Dhatuvamsa relates that the Buddha came to this spot with five hundred arahants on his third visit to the island, and that Kavantissa enshrined the forehead relic here in fulfilment of an old prophecy.

name: Muhudu Maha Vihara
significance: A ruined seaside monastery among the dunes at Pottuvil, held to have been founded more than two thousand years ago by King Kavan Tissa of Ruhuna. Remains of stupas, a seema malaka, an avasa geya and stone images of the Buddha and of kings or gods still stand on the site.
story: The Rajavaliya tells that Devi, daughter of the king of Kelaniya, was set adrift in a golden vessel to appease the sea gods and came ashore here, later marrying Kavan Tissa as Queen Viharamahadevi.

name: Somawathiya Chaitya
deity: Right canine tooth relic of Gautama Buddha
significance: A stupa on the Mahaweli floodplain in Polonnaruwa District, built in the reign of King Kavan Tissa by Prince Giri Abhaya to enshrine the Buddha's right canine tooth relic, which he received from Arahat Mahinda. It takes its name from the prince's wife, Princess Somawathi, sister of the king, and the couple handed the completed shrine to the monks.

name: Tai Pei Yuen Temple
significance: A Buddhist temple in Singapore's Balestier district, founded in 1938 as the Kuan Yin lodge by Chow Siew Keng, who had come from Guangdong two years earlier, and rebuilt in 1964. Under later abbesses it became known for charitable work, running a free clinic from 1980 and distributing rice dumplings to welfare homes from 1984.

name: Kadadora Vihara
significance: A Buddhist temple in the Kotmale valley whose garbhagriha held the principal Buddha image and whose walls carried paintings of the Buddha's life and the Jataka tales. It was abandoned in 1979 for the building of the Kotmale dam and drowned when the reservoir filled in 1985, one of some 54 religious sites lost with 57 villages.

name: Diệu Đế Temple
deity: Gautama Buddha, flanked by Samantabhadra and Manjushri
significance: A Buddhist pagoda on the Dong Ba Canal in Huế, facing the imperial citadel, built under the Nguyễn emperor Thiệu Trị, who named it for the Four Noble Truths and declared it one of Vietnam's national pagodas. It is known for the four low towers set about its gate and sanctuary.

name: Lankatilaka Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha, with devales to Upulvan, Ganapathi, Saman, Vibhishana, Kataragama and Kumara Bandara
significance: A rock-built temple near Pilimatalawa raised in the reign of Bhuvanekabahu IV and overseen by his chief minister Senalankadhikara, regarded as the finest building of the Gampola period. Designed by the South Indian architect Sathapati Rayar with Pandya sculptors from Tamil Nadu, it sets a Buddha image among six Hindu devales and was declared a protected monument in 1949.

name: Le-myet-hna Temple
deity: Eight seated Buddhas around the central pillar
significance: A four-sided black sandstone shrine at the northwest corner of the Shite-thaung temple in Mrauk U, completed in 1430 for King Min Saw Mon. Doorways on all four sides lead to a central pillar ringed by eight seated Buddhas.

name: Thatta Thattaha Maha Bawdi Pagoda
significance: A 49-metre pagoda in Naypyidaw built by the city's development committee as a full replica of the Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya, its principal Buddha image consecrated in May 2014 and the pagoda finished in 2015. The grounds also reproduce the sites of the Buddha's birth, enlightenment, first sermon and passing, for worshippers who cannot make the pilgrimage to India.

name: Chaukhtatgyi Buddha Temple
significance: A Yangon shrine holding one of Myanmar's most venerated reclining Buddha images, 66 metres long. Sir Po Tha paid for the first image in 1899 and it was finished in 1907, but its proportions and stern face were judged wrong; it was pulled down in the 1950s and the replacement, carved under the Dawei master U Thaung with glass eyes made at the Naga Glass Factory, was consecrated in 1973.

name: Wat Chetawan
significance: A Thai Theravada temple in Petaling Jaya founded in 1957 by Phra Kru Palat Vieng and designed by Thailand's Fine Arts Department, its gilded main shrine completed in June 1962 with funds to which King Bhumibol Adulyadej personally contributed. It holds a share of the Buddha relics excavated at Piprahwa in 1898, given by Lord Curzon to King Chulalongkorn of Siam and passed to Malaysia in 2012.

name: Mingun Pahtodawgyi
significance: A colossal brick stupa about 10 km northwest of Mandalay, begun by King Bodawpaya in 1790 and deliberately left unfinished; a small shrine with a Buddha image on the site is still used for worship.
story: It was said locally that the country would be lost, or in another telling that the king would die, the moment the pagoda was completed, so the work was slowed and then abandoned.

name: Báo Quốc Temple
deity: Gautama Buddha (triple Buddha statue; relics of the Buddha)
significance: A Thiền (Vietnamese Zen) temple on Hàm Long hill in Huế, founded in 1670 by the master Thích Giác Phong under the Nguyễn lords and enlarged from 1808 with the patronage of Empress Hiếu Khương, wife of Gia Long. Its triple gate, dragon-wound pillars and stupas stand above a spring that runs down into the grounds.

name: Bửu Phong Temple
significance: A Zen temple on a hill about 4 km from Biên Hòa, begun in the 17th century as a small shrine by Thích Bửu Phong, rebuilt by Chinese Buddhist settlers late in the 18th century, renovated in 1760 by Thích Viên Quang and enlarged in 1829 on donations from Nguyễn Văn Hiệp and Nguyễn Văn Tâm. Its main hall keeps an old statue of Amitabha, and a stupa on the grounds holds Buddhist relics.

name: Wat Phothivihan
significance: A Thai Theravada temple in Tumpat district, Kelantan, founded in 1973 by the abbot Phra Krurasapia Chakorn and known for its 40-metre reclining Buddha, begun in 1975 and finished in 1979. The grounds also hold an eighteen-armed Avalokiteshvara and a four-faced Phra Phrom, mixing Chinese and Tibetan elements into a Thai temple.

name: Siong Lim Temple
significance: Singapore's largest Chinese Mahayana temple complex, founded in 1898 by the Hokkien merchant Low Kim Pong and built between 1902 and 1907 at a cost of half a million dollars, modelled on Xi Chan Si in Fuzhou and blending Fuzhou, Quanzhou and Zhangzhou building traditions. It was gazetted a national monument in 1980.
story: Low Kim Pong is said to have dreamt of a golden light rising from the sea to the west, and on meeting a Buddhist family who landed by boat soon after, promised to build them a temple; their head became its first abbot.

name: Trúc Lâm Monastery
deity: Gautama Buddha, flanked by Văn Thù Sư Lợi and Phổ Hiền
significance: A Trúc Lâm Zen monastery above Da Lat, designed by the architects Ngô Viết Thụ and Nguyễn Tín and opened in March 1994. Its main hall holds a Gautama Buddha on a lotus between the bodhisattvas Văn Thù Sư Lợi and Phổ Hiền, and the community revives the Vietnamese Zen school founded by the Trần emperor Trần Nhân Tông, who gave up the throne to become a monk.

name: Kuanyin Si Temple
significance: A Chinese Buddhist temple on Chinatown Road in Amarapura, built in 1773 in the reign of King Singu with money from Chinese officials of the Burmese court, among them the tax minister Min Haw Hot. Burned three times between 1810 and 1837, it was rebuilt from 1838 under Tharrawaddy and finished in 1847 under King Pagan, with tall brick firebreak walls, and is treated as a monument of Burmese-Chinese exchange.

name: Thanboddhay Pagoda
significance: A Theravada pagoda near Monywa begun on 20 June 1939 by the Venerable Mohnyin Thambuddhei Sayadaw, paid for by local devotees and finished on 2 March 1952 on the site of a vanished 14th-century monastery. Its builder took the terraced form of Borobudur as his model, and the complex holds more than 580,000 Buddha images; during the Second World War its grounds sheltered thousands of refugees.

name: Linh Phước Temple
significance: A Buddhist temple at Trại Mát, 8 km from the centre of Da Lat, built between 1949 and 1952 and greatly enlarged after 1990 by the Venerable Thích Tâm Vị. It is known for mosaic work made from broken pottery and glass bottles, including a dragon whose open mouth shelters a Maitreya Buddha.
